denomProfiles/georgian-orthodox/tagline: Ancient church of St Nino and one of Georgia's most trusted institutions.
denomProfiles/georgian-orthodox/coreDoct: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Treasures its conversion through St Nino in the 330s and its tradition of apostolic preaching by Andrew.
Its autocephaly, dating from Antiochene grants in the early medieval period, was abolished by Russia in 1811, restored in 1917 and recognised by Constantinople in 1990.
Sees Orthodoxy as inseparable from Georgian language, culture and statehood.
denomProfiles/georgian-orthodox/focuses/: National and cultural identity, especially since independence in 1991.
Monastic revival and church building after the Soviet era.
Family and demographic concerns, such as the Patriarch's mass baptisms of third and later children since 2008.
Conservative moral teaching in public debates.
denomProfiles/georgian-orthodox/practice: Byzantine liturgy in Georgian, with distinctive polyphonic chant.
Led by the Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia, a title used since the 11th century; Ilia II was enthroned in 1977.
The grapevine cross of St Nino is the church's emblem; Svetitskhoveli Cathedral in Mtskheta is its mother church.
denomProfiles/georgian-orthodox/influenc: Georgian monks founded Iviron on Mount Athos and the Monastery of the Cross in Jerusalem.
Georgian script and literature developed largely through Bible translation and hagiography.
denomProfiles/georgian-orthodox/keyFigur: Woman evangelist who converted the royal house in the 4th century.
King of Iberia, first Christian ruler of Georgia.
12th-century king who founded Gelati Monastery and reformed the church.
Catholicos-Patriarch enthroned in 1977, central to the church's post-Soviet revival.
denomProfiles/georgian-orthodox/members/: About 83% of Georgia's population declared Orthodox in the 2014 census of the National Statistics Office of Georgia.
denomProfiles/cypriot-orthodox/tagline: Apostolic church of Barnabas, autocephalous since the Council of Ephesus.
denomProfiles/cypriot-orthodox/coreDoctr: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Traces its foundation to the apostles Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13).
Its independence from Antioch was confirmed by canon 8 of the Council of Ephesus (431).
Emperor Zeno confirmed its autocephaly in 488 after Barnabas's relics were reportedly found.
denomProfiles/cypriot-orthodox/focuses/0: Leadership of the Greek Cypriot community, inherited from the Ottoman role of the Archbishop as ethnarch.
denomProfiles/cypriot-orthodox/focuses/1: Care for churches and monasteries in the north, inaccessible or damaged since the Turkish invasion of 1974.
denomProfiles/cypriot-orthodox/focuses/2: Monastic centres such as Kykkos Monastery.
denomProfiles/cypriot-orthodox/focuses/3: Education and charitable work, supported by substantial church property.
denomProfiles/cypriot-orthodox/practices: The Archbishop keeps imperial privileges granted by Zeno: signing in red ink, carrying a sceptre and wearing a purple cloak.
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts.
The Archbishop of Nova Justiniana and All Cyprus is elected with lay participation.
denomProfiles/cypriot-orthodox/influence: Archbishop Makarios III led the struggle for independence and became the republic's first president in 1960.
Archbishop Chrysostomos II recognised the OCU in 2020, a decision that divided the Cypriot synod.
denomProfiles/cypriot-orthodox/keyFigure: Apostle and native of Cyprus, venerated as founder of the church.
Archbishop (1950–77) and first President of Cyprus.
Archbishop from 2006 until his death in 2022.
denomProfiles/polish-orthodox/tagline: Minority Orthodox church of Poland's east, rooted among Belarusians, Ukrainians and Lemkos.
denomProfiles/polish-orthodox/coreDoctri: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Received autocephaly from Constantinople in 1924, arguing that Kyiv's transfer to Moscow in 1686 had been uncanonical.
Moscow, which had rejected the 1924 grant, issued its own grant of autocephaly in 1948.
Has declined to recognise the Orthodox Church of Ukraine.
denomProfiles/polish-orthodox/focuses/0: Preserving the faith of national minorities in a predominantly Catholic country.
denomProfiles/polish-orthodox/focuses/1: Pilgrimage and spiritual life centred on the Holy Mountain of Grabarka.
denomProfiles/polish-orthodox/focuses/2: Theological education at the Christian Theological Academy in Warsaw.
denomProfiles/polish-orthodox/focuses/3: Remembrance of 20th-century suffering, including the destruction of churches in the 1930s and the deportations of 1947.
denomProfiles/polish-orthodox/practices/: Byzantine liturgy in Church Slavonic, with growing use of Polish.
The annual pilgrimage to Grabarka on the feast of the Transfiguration (19 August), where pilgrims leave crosses.
Led by the Metropolitan of Warsaw and All Poland; Metropolitan Sawa (Hrycuniak) has served since 1998.
denomProfiles/polish-orthodox/influenced: Orthodox of Czech Lands and Slovakia
Its bishops helped establish the hierarchy of the Orthodox Church of the Czech Lands and Slovakia after 1945.
Belarusian and Lemko culture in Poland
Parishes are centres of minority language and culture in Podlasie and elsewhere.
denomProfiles/polish-orthodox/keyFigures: Metropolitan of Warsaw who led the church to autocephaly in 1924.
Metropolitan of Warsaw and All Poland since 1998.
denomProfiles/albanian-orthodox/tagline: Church rebuilt from near-extinction after Albania's state atheism.
denomProfiles/albanian-orthodox/coreDoct: Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Proclaimed autocephaly at the Congress of Berat (1922), recognised by Constantinople in 1937.
Stresses Albanian-language worship as part of its national and pastoral identity.
Under Anastasios developed a theology of mission, reconciliation and interfaith respect in a Muslim-majority society.
denomProfiles/albanian-orthodox/focuses/: Rebuilding parishes, churches and clergy after the total ban on religion (1967–90).
Education, healthcare and social services open to all Albanians.
Peaceful coexistence with Muslims and Catholics.
Training a new generation of clergy at the Resurrection of Christ Theological Academy at Shën Vlash near Durrës.
denomProfiles/albanian-orthodox/practice: Byzantine liturgy in Albanian and Greek.
Uses the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts.
The Resurrection Cathedral in Tirana (consecrated 2014) symbolises the church's revival.
Led by the Archbishop of Tirana, Durrës and All Albania with the Holy Synod.
denomProfiles/albanian-orthodox/influenc: Anastasios's experience in Africa and Albania influenced Orthodox thinking on mission worldwide.
The vernacular liturgy contributed to the Albanian national awakening in the early 20th century.
denomProfiles/albanian-orthodox/keyFigur: Priest, statesman and translator who led the Albanian Orthodox movement.
First Archbishop after recognition of autocephaly in 1937.
Archbishop from 1992 until his death in 2025, who rebuilt the church.
denomProfiles/orthodox-church-in-america: English-speaking American Orthodox church grown from the Russian mission to Alaska.
Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Received autocephaly from the Moscow Patriarchate in 1970; Constantinople and most other churches have not recognised it.
Holds that the Orthodox in North America should form one local, territorial church rather than ethnic jurisdictions.
Its liturgical theology, shaped by Alexander Schmemann, centres the Church on the Eucharist.
Mission to English-speaking Americans and converts.
Theological education at St Vladimir's (founded 1938) and St Tikhon's seminaries.
The goal of a unified American Orthodox church.
Liturgical renewal and frequent Communion.
Byzantine liturgy mainly in English, with some Church Slavonic, Romanian, Albanian and Spanish.
Most parishes use the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts.
Led by a Metropolitan of All America and Canada and a Holy Synod.
Includes ethnic dioceses (Romanian, Albanian, Bulgarian) alongside territorial ones.
American convert Orthodoxy
Its English-language life and seminaries attracted many American converts.
Liturgical theology
Schmemann's 'For the Life of the World' shaped Orthodox and Western liturgical thought.
Herman of Alaska
Valaam monk in Alaska; in 1970 the first saint canonised in America.
Innocent (Veniaminov)
Missionary bishop and translator in Alaska, later Metropolitan of Moscow.
Tikhon of Moscow
Archbishop in America (1898–1907) before becoming Patriarch.
Alexander Schmemann
Dean of St Vladimir's Seminary and liturgical theologian.
Alexis Toth
Former Greek Catholic priest who led many Rusyns into Orthodoxy.
denomProfiles/orthodox-church-of-ukraine: Ukrainian autocephalous church recognised by Constantinople in 2019.
Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Holds, with Constantinople, that Kyiv was never canonically transferred to Moscow and that Constantinople could grant autocephaly.
Its Tomos (January 2019) makes it autocephalous but leaves Constantinople the preparation of the holy myron and certain appeals.
Rejects the 'Russian world' ideology as incompatible with Orthodox teaching.
Ukrainian national and spiritual independence, especially since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Receiving parishes that leave the Moscow-linked Ukrainian Orthodox Church.
Ukrainian-language worship and church life.
Pastoral care of soldiers, refugees and victims of war.
Byzantine liturgy in Ukrainian, with some Church Slavonic.
Moved to the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts on 1 September 2023, so Christmas falls on 25 December.
Led by the Metropolitan of Kyiv and All Ukraine; Epiphanius (Dumenko) was elected in 2018.
Recognised by Constantinople, Alexandria, Greece and Cyprus; Moscow and most other churches do not recognise it.
Debate on autocephaly
Its creation provoked a split between Moscow and Constantinople and a wider argument over who may grant autocephaly.
Vladimir (Volodymyr) the Great
Prince of Kyiv whose baptism (988) Ukrainians claim as their own origin.
Bartholomew I
Ecumenical Patriarch who signed the Tomos in 2019.
Epiphanius (Dumenko)
Metropolitan of Kyiv and All Ukraine since 2018.
Filaret (Denysenko)
Former head of the Kyiv Patriarchate who supported union but later withdrew.
denomProfiles/old-believers/tagline: Russian Orthodox who kept the pre-1650s rites after Nikon's reforms.
denomProfiles/old-believers/coreDoctrine: Hold that the pre-Nikonian rites and books, inherited from Muscovite tradition, preserve the true Orthodox faith unchanged.
Saw Nikon's reforms and the anathemas of the 1666–67 councils as apostasy; some interpreted them as signs of the end times.
Priestly groups (popovtsy) retain bishops and the Eucharist; the Belokrinitsa hierarchy dates from 1846.
Priestless groups (bezpopovtsy) hold that valid priesthood ended, and practise lay-led worship without the Eucharist.
denomProfiles/old-believers/focuses/0: Faithful preservation of liturgical forms, chant, icons and manuscripts.
denomProfiles/old-believers/focuses/1: Communal discipline and separation from 'the world'.
denomProfiles/old-believers/focuses/2: Memory of martyrs such as Archpriest Avvakum and Boyarina Morozova.
denomProfiles/old-believers/focuses/3: Economic self-reliance; Old Believer merchants and industrialists were prominent in 19th-century Russia.
denomProfiles/old-believers/practices/0: Sign of the cross with two fingers and a double, not triple, Alleluia.
denomProfiles/old-believers/practices/1: Use of pre-reform service books, znamenny chant and the eight-pointed cross.
denomProfiles/old-believers/practices/2: Baptism by full triple immersion; men often wear beards.
denomProfiles/old-believers/practices/3: Communities in Russia, the Baltic states, Romania (Lipovans) and in the Americas and Australia.
denomProfiles/old-believers/practices/4: Some are in communion with the Moscow Patriarchate under the Edinoverie arrangement of 1800.
denomProfiles/old-believers/influenced/0: It lifted the anathemas on the old rites in 1971 and tolerates them within the Edinoverie.
denomProfiles/old-believers/influenced/1: Old Believer collectors preserved many icons and manuscripts and patronised Russian art.
denomProfiles/old-believers/keyFigures/0: Archpriest and author of an autobiographical Life, burned in 1682.
denomProfiles/old-believers/keyFigures/1: Noblewoman who died in prison in 1675, painted by Surikov.
denomProfiles/old-believers/keyFigures/2: Leader of the priestless Vyg community in northern Russia.
denomProfiles/old-believers/keyFigures/3: Former Metropolitan of Sarajevo whose joining in 1846 gave priestly Old Believers a hierarchy.
